currentFocus.label: Currently reading
currentFocus.text: How consumer memory survives personalization, claim saturation, and category sameness.

signalSystem.label: Signal room
signalSystem.headline: A project is useful when the signal can travel from evidence to product, brand, and marketing decisions.

lenses.label: collection
lenses.text: Some people do not stay loyal to a fragrance. They build a collection that says who they are becoming.

lenses.label: identity
lenses.text: Beauty is not only applied. It is assembled through planes, edges, colors, and permission.

lenses.label: category noise
lenses.text: When every brand says protein, gut health, and better-for-you, stated preference becomes crowded evidence.

lenses.label: memory
lenses.text: AI can personalize the journey, but brand meaning has to stay stable enough to be remembered.

lenses.label: infrastructure
lenses.text: Shared data can improve service, but the front-of-house behavior still has to feel specific to the house.

lenses.label: position
lenses.text: A crowded category is easier to read when you look for the position people can describe in one sentence.

fieldNotes.title: SIARA House
fieldNotes.text: Reading contemporary Indian jewellery through the positions that are already crowded: heritage, occasion, investment, and minimal everyday luxury. The open question is where a house can feel precise without becoming cold.

fieldNotes.title: The Permanence Paradox
fieldNotes.text: In fragrance, permanence is emotional before it is technical. A scent can last on skin and still fail to last in memory if the object, story, and social signal do not hold together.

fieldNotes.title: Sampling as collectibility
fieldNotes.text: Reading beauty sampling as a collectibility signal, not just a discovery mechanic. The interesting question is when a trial object becomes something people keep, show, or arrange.

statusGroups.label: Expanded highlights
statusGroups.text: Miutine, Givenchy, 19h03, Danone, L'Oréal, and LVMH have expanded read panels below. They are pulled from the same case data as the archive, so the tour and the system stay aligned.

statusGroups.label: Field notes and live inquiries
statusGroups.text: SIARA House, The Permanence Paradox, Attention vs Meaning, and the Claim Saturation Framework are kept visible as shorter notes until their evidence base deserves a full dossier.

cases.title: What AI Can't Personalize
cases.field: L'Oréal / AI and recognizable beauty codes
cases.label: Rule
cases.hook: What must stay recognizable when AI adapts beauty discovery?
cases.proof: Active inquiry on what should stay recognizable when AI adapts the beauty journey.
cases.hoverDetail: A rule set for separating adaptive utility from stable brand cues.

signature.behavior: Consumers accept adaptive help, but still look for cues that feel recognizably L'Oréal.
signature.evidence: Personalization patterns, beauty journey examples, and recognizable code mapping.
signature.tension: If every touchpoint changes for the individual, the brand can become useful but forgettable.
signature.system: A rule set separating adaptive surfaces from stable brand cues.

detail.heading: What AI Can't Personalize
detail.kicker: As AI personalizes discovery, beauty brands still need cues that stay recognizable.
detail.context: This is an inquiry about restraint. If every message, recommendation, and journey adapts to the individual, the brand still needs fixed cues people can recognize without thinking too hard.
fields: What must remain consistent for a beauty brand to stay recognizable across personalized journeys?
The closer something is to memory, the less it should be personalized. The closer something is to utility, the more it can adapt.
Consumers want recognition without being reduced to past clicks.
A rule set for separating adaptive utility from stable brand cues.
Beauty examples where personalization improves usefulness, plus examples where it weakens recognition.
Personalization strategy needs memory cues, not just targeting accuracy.

cases.title: Collectibility Over Loyalty
cases.label: Evidence
cases.hook: Why some fragrances become identity while others become collection.
cases.note: 4,700+ reviews revealed strong object value and weaker identity attachment.
cases.proof: 4,700+ reviews, competitive benchmarking, and social listening shaped an Identity Value x Object Value framework.
cases.hoverDetail: Strongest evidence anchor: review mining, competitive read, social listening, and recommendations.

signature.behavior: Consumers admired the object and collected the brand world, even when identity attachment was weaker.
signature.evidence: 4,700+ reviews, competitive benchmarks, attribute mining, and social listening.
signature.tension: A fragrance can be visible and desirable without becoming a signature scent.
signature.move: Separate object value from identity value.
signature.system: A framework for deciding whether to build collectibility, loyalty, or both.

detail.heading: Collectibility Over Loyalty
detail.kicker: Why Miutine behaves more like a luxury object than a signature fragrance.
detail.context: This is the evidence anchor of the portfolio. The work started with a concrete dataset and used consumer language to separate being admired, being collected, and being personally adopted.
fields: 4,700+ reviews, competitive benchmarks, attribute-level review mining, and Instagram plus TikTok social listening.
Consumers praised the bottle and object codes even when longevity weakened attachment.
Visibility and satisfaction were present, but identity drivers like confidence, sex appeal, and compliments were weaker.
Identity Value x Object Value separated collectible appeal from signature-fragrance attachment.
Review mining, competitive read, social listening, framework, and recommendations.
Full evidence-backed case now in the portfolio.

cases.title: Attention vs Meaning
cases.label: Question
cases.hook: Can beauty brands measure durable meaning as well as engagement?
cases.note: Clicks show attention. Repeatable cues show memory.
cases.proof: A measurement question for when engagement becomes a noisy proxy for meaning.
cases.hoverDetail: Useful as a bridge between CRM metrics and recognizable cues.

cases.title: Claim Saturation
cases.label: Question
cases.hook: Which signals matter after every brand learns the same nutrition claims?
cases.note: When everyone has the same insight, which signals still matter?
cases.proof: Active inquiry on claim saturation in dairy and nutrition, built from category trend analysis.
cases.hoverDetail: Next proof: category map, claim audit, shelf examples, and behavior gaps.

signature.behavior: Consumers say they want the same health benefits every brand now knows how to claim.
signature.evidence: Category trend reading, claim convergence, shelf language, and behavior-gap mapping.
signature.tension: Research can start measuring category noise instead of useful differentiation.
signature.move: Look for the behavior that contradicts the claim.
signature.system: A prioritization model for deciding which claims deserve product and marketing weight.

detail.heading: Claim Saturation
detail.kicker: When every competitor learns the same nutrition insight, which signals are still worth researching?
detail.context: This is deliberately marked as an inquiry, not a finished case. The open question is how a food brand can avoid chasing the same claims everyone else has already learned to make.
fields: Protein, probiotics, reformulation, and better-for-you benefits are converging across dairy and adjacent nutrition.
Consumer work can start measuring category-wide noise instead of useful differentiation.
Look for where behavior contradicts stated preference: what people buy, repeat, trade off, or ignore.
Framework outline for consumer insight, category reading, and claim-space prioritization.
Category map, claim audit, shelf examples, and sharper evidence on where stated preference and buying behavior diverge.
Category saturation can become a research question, not just a positioning problem.

cases.title: Claim Saturation Framework
cases.label: Framework
cases.hook: A reusable model for finding signal after category language converges.
cases.note: Move from claim audit to behavior gap to defensible choice cue.
cases.proof: A reusable model for reading categories where everyone has learned the same benefits.
cases.hoverDetail: Keeps Danone from reading like a one-off and turns it into transferable method.

cases.title: Shared Infrastructure, House-Specific Expression
cases.label: Tension
cases.hook: Can luxury groups share intelligence without flattening the houses?
cases.note: Scale the intelligence without flattening the house.
cases.proof: Active inquiry on sharing customer intelligence without making every house behave the same.
cases.hoverDetail: A group-level CRM question that keeps house codes as a design constraint.

signature.behavior: Luxury customers can benefit from better memory across houses, but still expect each house to behave distinctly.
signature.evidence: Luxury service moments, house code mapping, CRM use cases, and portfolio logic.
signature.tension: Shared intelligence can improve relevance while flattening the houses it is meant to support.
signature.system: A group-level CRM logic with house-specific rules at the customer-facing layer.

detail.heading: Shared Infrastructure, House-Specific Expression
detail.kicker: Can luxury groups share customer intelligence without making every house feel the same?
detail.context: This stays separate from Givenchy. Givenchy is a house-level product and identity territory. LVMH is a group-level question about what can be shared behind the scenes while each house keeps its own behavior in front of the customer.
fields: Shared data can improve CRM, service, and relevance across a luxury portfolio.
The same efficiency can flatten house memory if every brand starts behaving alike.
This is group-level infrastructure thinking, distinct from Givenchy's house-level product territory.
House code map, service moments, and customer use cases that show where shared data should stop.
Good data architecture has to protect meaning, not just increase efficiency.

cases.title: Givenchy Face Architecture
cases.label: Move
cases.hook: How couture construction became a defensible beauty territory.
cases.note: Makeup became identity construction, not surface decoration.
cases.proof: Couture construction became a face architecture territory, presented to the Givenchy beauty team.
cases.hoverDetail: Finished concept dossier with positioning, concept system, experience logic, and service cues.

signature.behavior: Beauty consumers assemble identity through planes, colors, edges, and permission.
signature.evidence: Couture codes, competitive beauty territories, product architecture, and presented concept work.
signature.tension: Couture authority is strong, but beauty needs a repeatable house logic beyond fashion adjacency.
signature.system: A territory that organizes product, service, ritual, and seasonal expression.

detail.heading: Face Architecture
detail.kicker: A beauty territory that translates couture construction into product, service, ritual, and seasonal expression.
detail.context: The point was not simply to say couture can inspire makeup. The work asked what Givenchy could own in beauty that competitors could not borrow as easily: the construction of the face as a repeatable house logic.
fields: Beauty consumers use the face to construct identity through plane, line, volume, and accent.
Couture had authority, but beauty needed a repeatable meaning beyond fashion adjacency.
Turn the face into architecture and make construction the organizing idea.
Positioning, concept system, experience logic, and service cues.
Finished concept dossier, presented as a sprint to the Givenchy beauty team.
Consumer identity can become a product and brand system.

cases.title: The Permanence Paradox
cases.label: Tension
cases.hook: What remains defensible when scent itself becomes easy to copy?
cases.note: Longevity on skin and longevity in memory are not the same problem.
cases.proof: A fragrance strategy note connected to the Miutine evidence base.
cases.hoverDetail: Useful for reading how object, story, and social signal make scent more durable.

cases.title: 19h03: The Third Hour
cases.label: Ritual
cases.hook: Can the overlooked hour after work become a branded ritual?
cases.note: People use the first drink to mark a change of state.
cases.proof: A finished concept dossier showing how one occasion can organize product benefit, social meaning, visual codes, and brand world.
cases.hoverDetail: Turns the first evening drink into product logic and brand atmosphere.

signature.behavior: People use the first drink to mark a change of state before they think about flavor.
signature.evidence: Occasion reading, ritual analysis, category gaps, and concept development.
signature.tension: Non-alcoholic and functional drinks often define themselves by what is missing.
signature.move: Own the third hour instead of the substitute category.
signature.system: A product ritual that connects benefit, occasion, visual code, and brand world.

detail.heading: 19h03
detail.kicker: A functional sparkling aperitif built around the precise moment the day becomes evening.
detail.context: This is a finished concept dossier rather than a research-heavy case. It shows how one occasion, the first evening drink, can organize product benefit, social meaning, visual codes, and brand world.
fields: People use the first drink as a social and emotional transition.
Non-alcoholic and functional drinks often define themselves by what is missing.
Own the moment of transition rather than the substitute category.
Occasion insight, product concept, positioning, and brand atmosphere.
Finished concept dossier showing how a behavior becomes product logic and brand world.
Consumer ritual can become a product proposition.

cases.title: SIARA House
cases.label: Position
cases.hook: Where is the least crowded position in contemporary Indian jewellery?
cases.note: The useful position has to be memorable before it is ornamental.
cases.proof: A live positioning note for contemporary Indian jewellery.
cases.hoverDetail: Uses the same territory discipline as Givenchy, applied to a different category.
